issues.legal_issue: An arbitrator appointed under one of two independent agreements lacks authority to decide disputes arising under the other agreement unless those disputes fall within the arbitration submission.
material_facts: The parties entered into separate lease and dealership agreements, each with its own arbitration clause and designated appointing authority.
The respondent invoked the dealership agreement’s arbitration clause, and an arbitrator was appointed under that clause.
The arbitrator nevertheless decided disputes about the lease, including the lease rent and lease period.
The appellant objected that the respondent’s requested change to the lease rent was outside the arbitration proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The arbitrator appointed under the dealership agreement had no authority to decide disputes under the separate lease agreement. The award changing the lease rent and lease period dealt with matters beyond the submission to arbitration and was set aside to that extent.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 34(2)(a)(iv) and 34(2)(a)(v) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an award may be set aside to the extent it decides matters beyond the submission, and the tribunal’s composition or procedure must accord with the applicable agreement. An arbitral tribunal is a creature of contract and must act within the authority conferred by the agreement under which it is constituted. The Court relied on Rahul Yadav v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. for the independence of lease and dealership agreements.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party seeks judicial review of an arbitral award.
predicates.agreements_have_separate_arbitration_ter: The parties made distinct agreements that provide for separate arbitration arrangements.
predicates.arbitrator_appointed_under_one_agreement: The arbitrator was appointed under the arbitration arrangement in one of the agreements.
predicates.award_decides_dispute_under_other_agreem: The arbitrator decided a dispute arising under the other agreement.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an award and the arbitrator appointed under one agreement decides a dispute under another agreement with separate arbitration terms, the portion deciding that dispute is set aside as beyond the arbitration’s scope.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal cannot replace clear, agreed contractual terms with different terms, and an award doing so may be set aside on the limited grounds for judicial review of arbitral awards.
material_facts: The registered lease fixed the monthly rent and provided for a specified lease period.
The respondent sought an increase in rent and a change to the lease period in arbitration invoked under the separate dealership agreement.
The arbitrator increased the rent and reduced the lease period, although the lease terms had not been altered by agreement of the parties.
The respondent had entered into the lease voluntarily, and the tribunal had not found any term of the dealership agreement unconscionable.
issues.conclusion: The award’s changes to the lease rent and lease period were in patent disregard of the lease terms and were set aside. The parties remained bound by their agreed lease terms.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 restrict judicial intervention to the grounds specified in Section 34, including conflict with public policy under Section 34(2)(b)(ii) and, for applicable domestic awards, patent illegality under Section 34(2A). A court does not review the merits or reappraise evidence and ordinarily does not interfere with a reasonable contractual interpretation; however, an award that disregards the contract or rewrites it can be set aside. The Court relied on Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Co. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India, PSA SICAL Terminals Pvt. Ltd. v. Board of Trustees of V.O. Chidambranar Port Trust, M.D., Army Welfare Housing Organisation v. Sumangal Service (P) Ltd., and Satyanarayana Construction Co. v. Union of India. It distinguished Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly because the case concerned a voluntary lease, not an employment contract, and there was no finding of an unconscionable term.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party seeks judicial review of an arbitral award.
predicates.contract_terms_are_express: The parties’ contract states the terms governing the matter in dispute.
predicates.tribunal_changes_terms_without_party_agr: The tribunal awards terms different from those in the contract without the parties agreeing to the change.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an award, the contract states the governing terms, and the tribunal changes those terms without the parties’ agreement, the altered portion of the award is set aside.
